opus-5.5.text:
I think the common ground is actually broader than people outside the field might expect, even though from the outside it can look like everyone is fighting over different routes.

First, almost everyone agrees that the goal is a general-purpose robot: not a machine that does one task in one factory cell, but something that can perceive an open, unstructured environment, understand what a human wants, and then act physically to get it done. Whether you come from computer vision, from robotics control, from reinforcement learning, or from large language models, that's the shared north star.

Second, I think there's a consensus that data is the core bottleneck. In language, we had the internet, trillions of tokens just sitting there. In embodied AI, there is no "internet of robot actions." Every trajectory has to be collected, either by teleoperation, by simulation, or by learning from human videos. So the debate is really about *how* to get data at scale, and people disagree on the mix, but nobody disputes that data is the problem. My own view has been that synthetic data and simulation have to carry a large share of the load, because real-world collection alone is too slow and too expensive to reach the scale that generalization requires. Then you use a smaller amount of real data to close the sim-to-real gap.

Third, people agree that we need some form of foundation model for the body, something that plays the role for robotics that GPT played for language. What that looks like is still open. Is it a vision-language-action model end to end? Is it a layered system with a "brain" for planning and a "cerebellum" for fast, precise control? I lean toward thinking that, at least for now, a hierarchical structure is more practical, because high-level reasoning and low-level motor skills have very different requirements in frequency, precision, and data.

And finally, I'd say there's a shared sense of urgency and of humility. Everyone sees that this is the next big frontier after language models, and everyone also knows we're still early. Robots today can do impressive demos, but robust, reliable performance in a real home or a real store, day after day, is still hard. So the common ground is: same destination, data as the key constraint, a belief in foundation models, and an honest recognition that the hardest part, getting to real generalization in the physical world, is still ahead of us.

r001.rationale: The candidate identifies a shared goal of general-purpose robots and says data is the core bottleneck, while noting researchers disagree about how to scale data and which model structure to use.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the common ground is actually quite clear if you look at what everyone in this field is really chasing, even though the technical routes differ a lot.

First, everyone agrees that intelligence has to be grounded in interaction with the physical world. Whether you come from robotics, from computer vision, or from large language models, the shared belief is that perception, understanding, and action cannot be separated. A model that only reads text or only looks at images is missing the feedback loop that comes from actually touching, moving, and failing in a real environment. That is the philosophical consensus.

Second, I think almost everyone has accepted that data is the central bottleneck. In language and vision, the internet gave us essentially free data at scale. In embodied AI, there is no internet of robot actions. So whether people are doing teleoperation, simulation, synthetic data, learning from human videos, or real-world data collection, they are all answering the same question: where does the data come from, and how do we make it cheap and diverse enough. Our disagreements are about the path, not about the problem.

Third, there is a shared belief in generalization as the goal. Traditional robotics was very good at one task in one setting. What everyone in embodied AI wants now is a system that can go to a new kitchen, a new factory, a new object it has never seen, and still work. That is why people talk about foundation models for robots. Nobody wants to go back to hand-engineering each task.

And I would add a fourth point, which is more about the community itself. Most of us came from different fields, and I think there is a genuine recognition that no single discipline can solve this alone. You need people who understand hardware, control, learning, and also people who understand how to scale systems. So there is a kind of humility, at least among the serious researchers, that the problem is bigger than any one toolbox.

Where the real differences show up is in the sequencing. Some people believe you should scale real-world data first and worry about simulation later. Others, including myself to a large degree, believe simulation and synthetic data have to carry a lot of the weight because the real-world data cost is simply too high. But those are strategic bets layered on top of a shared foundation. The foundation is that intelligence must act in the world, that data is the constraint, and that generalization is the target.

r001.rationale: The response identifies data as the shared bottleneck in embodied AI and says researchers differ in their technical routes and data-collection strategies. This conveys common ground in pursuing data-driven embodied systems rather than agreeing on one approach.

astra-6.text:
I think the common ground is that intelligence has to be understood through interaction with the world. An embodied agent doesn’t just observe and produce an answer—it takes an action, changes its environment, and then uses the feedback to decide what to do next. Perception, decision-making, and action are connected in that loop.

Researchers may approach this from different directions. Some focus on robotics, some on learning algorithms, and others on simulation. We don’t necessarily agree on the best technical route. But I think we share the ambition of building agents that can handle new objects, new environments, and new tasks, rather than only succeeding in a carefully prepared setting.

For me, that’s the central question: how do we turn success on a particular task into a capability that carries over to the next situation?

r001.rationale: The response says researchers differ on technical routes and share the ambition to build agents that generalize across tasks, but it does not identify their common ground as pursuing data-driven robots.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the common ground is the belief that intelligence develops through interaction with the world. An embodied agent needs to connect perception, decision-making, and action: it observes something, acts, and then learns from what changes.

Researchers may focus on different parts—robotics, vision, learning, or simulation—but we share a central question: how can an agent use its experience to handle situations it hasn’t seen before? That also means paying attention to the body and the environment. What an agent can learn depends partly on what it can sense and what actions it can take.

So, for me, the shared goal is to bring those pieces together into a system that can act reliably and adapt through experience.

r001.rationale: The response describes learning through interaction and experience, and says researchers may focus on different areas. It does not clearly identify the common ground as pursuing data-driven robots.
